prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B016 to B014, and I want to be exact about why. It is not that six colleagues prefer B014; the chair is right that counting is no substitute for judgement. It is that the first-round exchange tested the two points on which I had made my own case conditional, and B016 did not survive them as well as B014 did. In round 1 I wrote that if the fairness gap in the B016 credit proved too large, B014 was the cleaner configuration. Danielsson, Johansson, Lindroth, Olsson and Mehlig each independently pressed the same fact: Molenkamp's HgTe experiment tested a prediction made by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Zhang cannot be credited, and the three-dimensional work lies outside the names. I cannot answer that with a three-name cut, so I accept that B016 is the stronger science but the less defensible prize this year. On the other side, my own question, whether the clock is an enabling instrument or tells us something new, has been answered more concretely than I expected: the magic-wavelength condition in the Lamb-Dicke regime is a single mechanism that explains why many neutral atoms can be interrogated with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed, and it has produced measured physics (centimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body clock effects, bounds on drifting constants). Above all it meets the reproducibility test I apply to everything, since JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST agree at about 1e-18. As a condensed-matter theorist I find the many-body interpretation of lattice-clock shifts a respectable piece of quantum matter physics in its own right. The credit is two names with a clear division between the proposal (Katori) and the realisation at record performance (Ye), and the citation should say invention and realisation so that it does not read as credit for the whole clock community.
statement.case_against: The reservations all remain. The comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes sit close, and a sceptical reader can call this a third prize for precision time; I think the distinction is defensible (an ensemble of neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled by design, as opposed to a ruler or a single ion), but it is a judgement and not a fact. The SI second has not been redefined, although I do not think a prize for an invention should wait on an administrative decision. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others are outside the two names, and I am recalling the priority history from colleagues and not from papers. Finally, I leave behind what I still think is the deepest concept on the list: a prize for B016 would have been a prize for a new class of quantum matter, and the committee should be aware that choosing the cleaner attribution means passing over it, perhaps for a year in which the HgTe and three-dimensional credit can be arranged more cleanly.

responses.point: Danielsson asks, with the chair, what fact would make Eriksson prefer B016 to B014, and argues that a prize omitting the proposers of the very experiment it rewards is not yet clean, while also holding that the clock is an instrument whose payoff is still ahead.
responses.response: On the chair's question to us both: I could not name a fact that would restore B016 above B014 within a three-person limit, because the missing person is the problem, and Zhang's death means the omission cannot be repaired. So on credit I now agree with you, and I have moved. On the other half of your argument I disagree. The clock has already given measured results, namely millimetre-to-centimetre gravitational redshift, many-body clock physics and bounds on constants, so it is not waiting for its science. I also share your wish to honour IceCube's pioneers while they are active; my reason for not putting B021 first is the one you and the chair both state, that confirmation lies within IceCube channels and the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the precursors is a judgement. That is a question for you and the chair rather than for me, and I would support an expert assessment on it before any future ballot.

responses.point: Johansson calls B016 conceptually the deepest candidate but ranks it behind B014 for attribution and prior recognition, would support it only if originality outweighed allocation tidiness, and wants the B014 citation to say invention and realisation.
responses.response: We now reach the same ordering for the same reason, and I adopt your drafting point: the citation should name the invention and the realisation and promise no applications. I do not accept the part of your case that rests on the 2016 prize, since the Z2 classification and the HgTe edge transport are distinct discoveries; the credit gap alone moves me. On B009, since I asked you in round 1 whether you should step back, thank you for the disclosure and for discounting your own first place. I would ask that the committee treat B009 as outside this year's ballot for the timing reasons Kroll, Mehlig and Lindroth give, which spares you from needing to recuse and does not require a view on its science.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the clock is a genuine conceptual step because magic-wavelength trapping combined with ultranarrow forbidden transitions controls projection noise and Doppler and recoil shifts together, and she says she may be too fond of a field close to her own.
responses.response: Her Lamb-Dicke argument is what answers my round-1 instrument-versus-discovery question, and I agree with her that it is a single idea and not a better clock. Because she is the member closest to the field, I want to take up the chair's question to her and say what I would regard as sufficient for a one-sentence distinction from 2005 and 2012: the comb provides the ruler and the ion work controls a single quantum system, whereas the lattice scheme interrogates a large neutral-atom ensemble with the light shift cancelled by design. If she can confirm that sentence, and the 2001-2003 priority dates, I am comfortable. I would not extend her three-name instinct toward Lemonde or Ludlow; adding a third name would weaken the clean division between proposal and realisation.

responses.point: Kroll supports B014 as a new measurement technique opening new observations, would not wait for the SI redefinition, and asks whether a B014 plus single-person B008 part is workable under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I now agree with him on the configuration, and we agree that the redefinition of the second should not be a precondition. I would still qualify one thing from my round-1 reply: I disputed that a measurement technique outranks a new state of matter, and I have not changed that view of the science; I have changed my ballot because of attribution. On two parts, I agree that B014 plus any part of B008 breaks the three-person limit at two plus at least one, and invites a split of the compound candidate between Blatt and Bloch that I cannot defend, so I would treat the final ballot as a choice among single-achievement prizes. I accept his point that his bias toward metrology is worth discounting, and I note that my own agreement rests on the credit and reproducibility argument and does not depend on that bias.

responses.point: Olsson places B016 below B014 and outside her alternatives because the committee cannot name with confidence the people who did the original work, and asks that the priority dates for the clock be checked before the citation is fixed.
responses.response: Her objection to B016 is the one I could not answer, and I now take it as decisive for this year. I would add that her own request, to check the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium demonstration against the record before fixing the citation, applies equally to my new position, and I support it. On B042, she is right to propose a recusal; I would add that the STEM-corrector omission (Krivanek) would remain a credit problem for a non-conflicted reader too, so the question is not only one of parochialism. I would ask her whether B017 would still be a serious later candidate if the pairing mechanism were better settled, since I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig finds the lattice clock persuasive because one mechanism explains it, argues the 2005 and 2012 prizes are distinguishable from it, and says that agreement on B014 rests on independent scientific arguments and not on shared impression.
responses.response: I accept his reading, and I would add the independent check that matters most to me: the clocks are reproduced by laboratories with different atoms and different groups and agree at the 1e-18 level. On B018, I take his point that Metzner's omission and the method-versus-discovery question keep DMFT below the clock, and I withdraw it from my own list as a result; my field proximity to LDA+DMFT is another reason not to advocate it. I would keep B017 in view as he suggests, since it is a better-defined theory-plus-experiment pair than DMFT, with the caveat that the pairing mechanism is not understood.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved B014 to the head of his configuration after reading the opening ballots, and the chair's observation warns that agreement on B014 is partly the result of members moving toward it.
responses.response: The warning applies to me and I should address it directly. I am one of the members who moved, and I have tried to say what moved me: the credit problem with B016 that five colleagues named, and the mechanistic and reproducibility argument for the clock. If either of those proved wrong, for instance if the priority dates do not hold for Katori, I would reopen my position. Support counts played no part. I would also support the chair's suggestion that the committee request expert checks on the priority dates and on IceCube's independent confirmation, since several of us, myself included, are working from recollection.

uncertainties: Whether the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal by Katori and the first lattice-clock demonstrations hold up against the documented record, and whether Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow or Takamoto have claims that make two names untenable; I am relying on colleagues' recollection.
Whether a prize committee can state, in one sentence, why the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes without sounding like a third prize for precision time.

Whether I have given too little weight to B016, which I still regard as the deepest conceptual candidate, by letting the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit gap decide this year; the argument for waiting is that a cleaner configuration may be available later.
Whether the pairing mechanism and sample variability in twisted bilayer graphene make B017 early, which affects how I treat my second alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B014 (Katori, Ye); I have no known collaboration with either, and atomic and optical clocks are far from my own work on electronic-structure theory and magnetism, so I defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson on priority history. My DFT and magnetism work is only broadly adjacent to B016 and is close to B018 (LDA+DMFT), and I have withdrawn B018 from my own list, so that proximity should not influence the ballot. I record that I moved from B016 to B014 in this round for the reasons above and not for consensus.
